source.title_on_document: FIERO: Empowering Creative Writing Through Collaborative Game Play

supplement.where: Appendices A-H, pp. 41-51 of this PDF; no separate external statistical supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Appendix A, Tables 1-2 (pp. 41-42), supplies questionnaire means, SDs, group Ns, Mann-Whitney z statistics, p values and effect sizes r. Appendix C, Tables 3-4 (pp. 43-44), lists participants. Appendix D (pp. 44-47) gives the LLM evaluation rubric and prompt; E (pp. 47-48) gives participant instructions; F, Table 5 (p. 49), gives models and decoding parameters; F-G (pp. 49-51) gives prompts and conflict-resolution details; H (p. 51) gives artifact information. No SEs or CIs for the scored-story outcomes are supplied.

paper_design_summary: In an offline, between-subjects experiment, 60 people were randomly assigned to FIERO or shared-Google-Docs collaborative writing and worked in teams of three on a superhero story (pp. 13-16, Sections 4.1-4.4). FIERO bundled physical cards and a game interface with generative-AI imagery, decision support, and story refinement; AI remained available during production of the final story (pp. 12-14 and 48-50). Three LLM judges compared the final stories on seven dimensions, while separate questionnaires measured participants' perceptions; the content analysis reports nine texts per arm despite recruitment and questionnaire results covering ten teams per arm (pp. 16-17, 27-29, and 41).

studies.label: User study: FIERO versus shared-document collaborative superhero writing

assignment.what_was_assigned: Participants were randomly assigned to FIERO or the control story-creation condition, then described as organized into teams of three. The randomization method and the sequence of team formation relative to assignment are not explained. The assigned FIERO condition bundles generative AI with physical cards and game-interface features (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 34, Section 6.6.1).
assignment.quote: In this between-subjects experiment, 60 participants were randomly assigned to either a story creation group or a card game-based story creation group.

arms.name: FIERO Group (Card Game Based Story Creation Group; G)
arms.description: Face-to-face teams write using FIERO, physical narrative cards, generated images, optional AI decision suggestions and final-story support. Same narrative tasks and round timing as control (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 48, Appendix E.2). n_analyzed is the questionnaire count (p. 41, Table 1); the story analysis uses nine texts (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Arm-specific assignment-stage counts are not explicitly stated.

arms.name: Control Group (Story Creation Group; C)
arms.description: Face-to-face teams use one shared Google Docs page for individual drafts, mutual review, oral discussion and integration. The baseline has no AI and no physical cards (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1; p. 34, Section 6.6.1; pp. 47-48, Appendix E.1). Human collaboration is present in both arms, so this is coded ai_vs_bau. n_analyzed is the questionnaire count (p. 41, Table 1); the story analysis uses nine texts (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). Arm-specific assignment-stage counts are not explicitly stated.

participants.exclusions: No participant exclusions or attrition reasons are reported. The reported analysis N is 30 people per arm for questionnaires (p. 41, Table 1), with ten teams of three recruited per arm (p. 16, Section 4.4). Content analysis instead uses nine texts per arm (p. 17, Section 4.5.2), without identifying omitted teams or explaining the discrepancy. The number of people represented in the scored-story subset is not explicitly stated and has not been inferred from the text count.
participants.who: Non-professional creators interested in collaborative writing but not considering themselves proficient; primarily students, with other participants working in technology, design, media, marketing and office roles. Recruited through word of mouth and social media; ages 18-28; no professional publishing or screenwriting backgrounds or prior creative-writing experience (p. 16, Section 4.4).
participants.quote: We recruited 30 participants for each of the Control and FIERO groups (divided into 10 teams of 3 members each) to take part in an offline collaborative writing activity.
participants.locator: p. 13, Section 4.1 (60 randomized); p. 16, Section 4.4 (recruitment and population); p. 41, Table 1 (30 analyzed per arm); pp. 42-44, Appendix C and Tables 3-4 (participant roster); p. 17, Section 4.5.2 (nine texts per arm).

ai_tool.name_model: FIERO: GPT-4 for decision support and final-story suggestions; GPT-4o image model (gpt-4o-image) for images (p. 12, Section 3.4; p. 49, Table 5).
ai_tool.how_used: The interface assembles player-authored drafts for optional AI selection and explanation of villain/weapon choices, story integration and polishing, and generates images from cards plus participants' text. Refinement is the main text-writing role, accompanied by image generation and decision support. Participants can accept, modify or ignore suggestions; final AI story support remains available while they complete the scored story (pp. 12-14, Sections 3.3.3-4.1; p. 48, Appendix E.2; pp. 49-51, Appendices F-G).

task.description: Teams of three collaboratively create a superhero story: individual hero/backstory creation, villain and scene development, weapon and climax development, and integration into a complete story (p. 13, Section 4.1; pp. 47-48, Appendix E).
task.duration: 30 minutes as stated in Section 4.1: three rounds, each with 5 minutes of individual thinking and 5 minutes of group discussion (p. 13). Appendix E (p. 48) lists final synthesis after the rounds but gives no separate duration.

outcomes.name: Creativity
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rubric assesses originality, innovative concepts, uniqueness, fresh perspectives, and imaginative content (pp. 15-16, Section 4.2.2; p. 46, Appendix D). Pairwise LLM-as-judge evaluation of final team-written stories by Claude Opus 4.5, Gemini 3 Pro, and GPT-5.2; model-specific results are retained as variants of one outcome. Each of nine FIERO texts is compared with each of nine control texts, in both AB and BA order; inconsistent decisions become draws (p. 17, Section 4.5.2). n_units = 81 text pairs per judge, not people or independent teams (p. 27, Section 5.4.1). Figure 14 reports percentage net advantage of FIERO over control. No participant- or team-adjusted SE or CI is reported.

Appendix D's JSON includes both Overall and Final_Winner fields (p. 47). The paper does not clearly map these fields to the two result summaries; both summaries are retained within this outcome rather than counted as independent outcomes. The Claude result differs between the summaries. The reported chi-squared tests concern Section 5.4.1's overall comparison; their treatment of repeated use of the same stories is not described. company_involvement.description: Coauthor Vince Siu is affiliated with Press Start Academy, a non-university organization. The document does not state AI-provider sponsorship, funding, or a separate commercial role.

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly reports random assignment of 60 people to an AI-enabled creative-writing system or a no-AI writing condition in supervised, face-to-face sessions (pp. 13-14, Section 4.1), and questionnaire analyses report 30 people per arm (p. 41, Table 1). Final team stories were scored for creativity and other narrative dimensions by LLM judges, satisfying the computed-output-measure criterion (pp. 15-17, Sections 4.2.2 and 4.5.2; pp. 27-29, Section 5.4 and Figures 13-14). Eligibility is based on the study-level reported sample, not the 81 pairwise comparisons; the unexplained nine-text-per-arm subset must be resolved before extracting participant counts for those outcomes. The intervention bundles AI with cards and game features and does not identify the effect of AI alone (p. 34, Section 6.6.1).

one_line_finding: FIERO's creativity net advantage was -27.2% for Claude, 50.6% for Gemini and -7.4% for GPT-5.2, while overall-preference net advantages favored FIERO across judges (45.7-65.4%; p. 29, Figure 14).
open_questions: Why does content analysis include nine texts per arm when ten teams per arm were recruited, and exactly which participants' stories were analyzed (p. 16, Section 4.4; p. 17, Section 4.5.2; pp. 43-44, Tables 3-4)?

Were individuals randomized before forming teams, or were pre-existing teams assigned together? Section 4.1 states that participants were randomly assigned but does not explain the allocation procedure (p. 13).

Do Section 5.4.1/Figure 13 and Figure 14's Overall row represent different output fields or a reporting error? Appendix D includes both Overall and Final_Winner; the Claude overall results are inconsistent between the summaries (pp. 27, 29, 47).

Can participant- or team-level uncertainty be obtained for the scored-story results? The reported overall chi-squared tests use repeated story comparisons without describing adjustment for dependence, and dimension-level results lack SEs or CIs (pp. 17, 27-29).
notes: Read the entire markdown, including Appendices A-H, and verified design, participant counts, models and every recorded result against the PDF. Figures 13-14 were inspected directly as in-memory PDF renders because their numeric labels are images; no effect sizes or unprinted counts were computed. All locators use PDF page numbers, which match the printed pagination. Seven scored-story dimensions are recorded, with evaluator-model variants grouped within each dimension. Overall comparison results and Overall Preference are retained in one outcome with the reporting ambiguity explicit. No outcome is explicitly designated primary. Questionnaire CSI, CSE and SSA measures are self-reports and are not included as scored-output outcomes; the abstract's idea-fluency and novelty-generation claims refer to those questionnaires (pp. 14-15, Sections 4.2.1-4.2.2; pp. 41-42, Tables 1-2). Qualitative observations of stereotypes, homogenization and narrative changes do not provide an across-people diversity score; there is no after-AI test. No shared participant sample or reanalysis of another paper is stated. Appendix G does not supply a distinct adversarial dataset or quantitative benchmark, despite the pre-deployment evaluation reference on p. 13; no additional study is counted (pp. 50-51). Appendix H identifies the code, cards and prompts repository but does not explicitly identify a participant/story dataset, so data_url is left empty (p. 51).
